content: 1. The evidence regarding the use of macrolides versus cephalosporins as prophylactic antibiotics for women undergoing cesarean section is of very low quality. This is due to a single study with design limitations, a small sample size, few events, and a wide confidence interval crossing the line of no effect. The estimated effect suggests 23 fewer infections per 1,000 women (ranging from 38 fewer to 313 more). 2. The comparison of gentamicin/nitroimidazole versus an antibiotic cocktail for prophylaxis in cesarean sections also shows very low-quality evidence. This is based on one study with design limitations, a small sample size, few events, and a wide confidence interval crossing the line of no effect. The estimated effect is 23 fewer infections per 1,000 women (ranging from 31 fewer to 44 more). 3. For the treatment of intra-amniotic infection/chorioamnionitis during labor, the evidence is of low quality. The findings are based on studies with design limitations, small sample sizes, and wide confidence intervals crossing the line of no effect. The estimated effect is 77 more infections per 1,000 women, but the data is not robust. 4. Postpartum treatment of intra-amniotic infection/chorioamnionitis with antibiotics shows very low-quality evidence. The estimated effect is 11 fewer infections per 1,000 women (ranging from 53 fewer to 167 more). The evidence is limited by design flaws, small sample sizes, and few events. 5. The comparison of once-daily versus thrice-daily gentamicin for postpartum intra-amniotic infection treatment is based on very low-quality evidence. The estimated effect is 30 more infections per 1,000 women, but the data is unreliable due to design limitations, small sample sizes, and wide confidence intervals. 6. The duration of antibiotic regimens for treating intra-amniotic infection (short versus long) is supported by very low-quality evidence. The studies contributing to the pooled effect had design limitations, small sample sizes, and wide confidence intervals crossing the line of no effect. 7. The use of ampicillin/gentamicin intrapartum versus postpartum for intra-amniotic infection treatment is based on very low-quality evidence. The estimated effect is 49 fewer infections per 1,000 women, but the data is unreliable due to serious design limitations, small sample sizes, and wide confidence intervals. 8. For postpartum endometritis, the comparison of lincosamides plus aminoglycosides versus other regimens shows very low-quality evidence. The estimated effect is six more infections per 1,000 women (ranging from three fewer to 73 more). The evidence is limited by design flaws and small sample sizes. 9. The use of aminoglycosides plus penicillin versus other regimens for postpartum endometritis treatment is supported by very low-quality evidence. The estimated effect is zero fewer infections per 1,000 women (ranging from 17 fewer to 119 more). The data is unreliable due to design limitations and small sample sizes. 10. The comparison of penicillin plus beta-lactamase inhibitors versus other regimens for postpartum endometritis treatment is based on very low-quality evidence. The estimated effect is 40 more infections per 1,000 women (ranging from six fewer to 438 more). The evidence is limited by design flaws and small sample sizes. 11. The use of aztreonam plus clindamycin versus other regimens for postpartum endometritis treatment is supported by very low-quality evidence. The estimated effect is 18 more infections per 1,000 women (ranging from 13 fewer to 354 more). The data is unreliable due to design limitations and small sample sizes. 12. The comparison of oral ofloxacin/clindamycin versus intravenous clindamycin/gentamicin for postpartum endometritis treatment is based on very low-quality evidence. The estimated effect is 124 fewer infections per 1,000 women (ranging from 319 fewer to 743 more). The evidence is limited by design flaws, small sample sizes, and wide confidence intervals. 13. The use of metronidazole plus gentamicin versus other regimens for postpartum endometritis treatment is supported by very low-quality evidence. The estimated effect is eight fewer infections per 1,000 women (ranging from 75 fewer to 301 more). The data is unreliable due to design limitations, small sample sizes, and few events. 14. The comparison of once-daily versus thrice-daily gentamicin for postpartum endometritis treatment shows moderate-quality evidence. The estimated effect is 20 fewer infections per 1,000 women, but the data is limited by design flaws and few events. 15. The continuation of oral antibiotics after an intravenous course for postpartum endometritis treatment is based on very low-quality evidence. The estimated effect is two more infections per 1,000 women, but the data is unreliable due to design limitations, small sample sizes, and few events. 16. The comparison of antibiotics with poor versus good activity against penicillinase-resistant bacteria for postpartum endometritis treatment is supported by low-quality evidence. The estimated effect is 73 more infections per 1,000 women, but the data is limited by design flaws, small sample sizes, and few events.
